setup.caption: 1. Find a touch-me-not plant with its leaves open.

setup.art: A feather touching the tip of one leaf, and the little leaflets folding together in pairs.
setup.caption: 2. Touch one leaf gently with a feather. Watch it fold.

setup.art: A child sitting by the plant with a phone timer showing minutes, the leaf half open again.
setup.caption: 3. Time how long it takes to open again.

flow.do: Find a touch-me-not plant with its leaves open. Look closely at one leaf.
flow.say: This plant is called chhui-mui, or lajwanti, or touch-me-not. Look at its little leaflets, lined up in pairs. What do you think will happen if we touch it?
flow.kid: This is a touch-me-not plant. Look at its tiny leaflets. What will happen if you touch it?
flow.context: This is the first step of the shy plant activity. You test whether a plant can sense touch.

flow.do: 1. Touch the tip of one leaf very gently with a feather. 2. Watch closely. 3. Start the timer.
flow.say: Gently now. Touch just the tip. Watch. What happens? Start the timer.
flow.kid: Touch the tip of one leaf with the feather. Watch it. Start the timer.
flow.parent: The leaflets fold together in a second or two, starting near the touch. Sometimes the fold spreads along the leaf, or the whole leaf drops. The plant does this by moving water out of special cells at the base of each leaflet. It is very fast for a plant.

check.q: When you touch a touch-me-not leaf, it folds shut. Which signs of life is it showing?
options: Sensing and movement
Nutrition and growth
Reproduction
check.why: The plant senses the touch and responds by moving its leaflets. That is sensing and movement. Picking 'nutrition and growth' mixes up a quick response with slow feeding and growing. Picking 'reproduction' means thinking any change is making young.

flow.do: 1. Choose a second leaf. Touch just the tip of one leaflet, as lightly as you can, with the feather. Count how many pairs fold. 2. Choose a third leaf. Tap its stalk firmly with one finger. Watch what happens.
flow.say: Let's compare. First the lightest touch you can make. How many pairs folded? Now a firm tap on another leaf. What is different?
flow.kid: Touch one leaflet very lightly. Count the pairs that fold. Then tap another leaf firmly. What is different?
flow.parent: A light touch usually folds only a few pairs near the tip. A firm tap folds the whole leaf, and the leaf stalk often droops down. The plant senses how strong the touch is, and responds more to a stronger one.

flow.do: Look at the first leaf every 5 minutes. Stop the timer when it is fully open again. Write down the minutes.
flow.say: Now we wait. Plants recover slowly. Let's check every 5 minutes. Meanwhile, why do you think the plant folds its leaves?
flow.kid: Look at the first leaf every 5 minutes. Stop the timer when it is open. Write down the minutes.
flow.parent: It often takes 10 to 30 minutes to open again. Good ideas for why: to scare off a hungry animal, to look less tasty, or to knock insects off. Scientists think it protects the plant from being eaten, but they are still testing this.

flow.do: Tell your child about J.C. Bose and the dropped plants. Then let the plant rest.
flow.say: J.C. Bose, a great Indian scientist, found that this plant folds less if you touch it again and again. In 2014, scientists dropped these plants gently many times. The plants stopped folding, and weeks later they still did not fold when dropped.
flow.kid: Scientists dropped these plants gently many times. The plants stopped folding. Weeks later, they still did not fold.
flow.think: DeepKids believes the plants learned that the drop was safe, and remembered it. Some scientists say the plants were only tired. What do you think?

activities.title: Does a plant give out water? The bag on a branch

materials.item: 2 clear plastic bags
2 rubber bands or pieces of string
a leafy plant in a pot, on a sunny windowsill or balcony
a dry dead twig of about the same size

activities.safety: Take the bags off within a few hours so the plant does not overheat. Never put a plastic bag near anyone's face.

schedule.what: Tie one bag over a leafy branch and one over a dead twig. Leave them in the sun for 2 hours. Compare the bags.

activities.record: Draw both bags after 2 hours. Write what you see inside each.
activities.context: This activity shows that a living plant takes in water and gives out water and gases through its leaves. You tie a bag over a living branch and another over a dead twig, and compare.

setup.art: A clear plastic bag tied with a rubber band over a leafy branch of a potted hibiscus on a sunny balcony.
setup.caption: 1. Tie a clear bag over a leafy, living branch.

setup.art: A second clear bag tied over a dry dead twig stuck in a pot of soil beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Tie another bag over a dead twig. Leave both in the sun.

setup.art: Two bags side by side after two hours: the leafy one misty with water drops, the twig one clear and dry.
setup.caption: 3. After 2 hours, compare the inside of the two bags.

flow.do: 1. Water the plant. 2. Slip a clear bag over one leafy branch and tie it gently. 3. Push a dead twig into the soil and tie a bag over it. 4. Leave both in sunlight.
flow.say: We have a living branch and a dead twig. Both get a bag. If the living plant gives anything out, the bag will catch it.
flow.kid: Tie a bag over a living branch. Tie another over a dead twig. Leave them in the sun.
flow.context: This is the first step of the bag-on-a-branch activity. You find out whether a living plant gives out water.

flow.do: After 2 hours, look at both bags. Touch the outside. Then take both bags off.
flow.say: Look! What is inside the bag on the living branch? And the dead twig's bag?
flow.kid: Look at the two bags. Which one has water drops inside?

check.q: After 2 hours in the sun, the bag on the living branch is misty with water, and the bag on the dead twig is dry. Why?
options: Rain got into the first bag
The living plant took water up from its roots and gave it out through its leaves
The dead twig drank all the water
check.why: A living plant pulls water up from its roots and lets water vapour out of tiny holes in its leaves. The vapour turns back into drops on the inside of the bag. The dead twig is once alive. It no longer does this. Picking 'rain' cannot explain why only one bag is wet. Picking 'the twig drank it' means thinking a dead twig still feeds.

flow.do: Talk about what the plant takes in and gives out.
flow.say: A plant takes in water and air. It gives out water vapour and gases from its leaves. In sunlight, one gas it gives out is oxygen, the gas we need.
flow.kid: A plant takes in water and air. It gives out water and gases from its leaves. One gas is oxygen, which we breathe.
flow.parent: Strictly, most of this water is not waste. The plant lets it out as it pulls up water and minerals from the soil, and it also cools the leaves. True plant waste includes the oxygen it makes in sunlight, carbon dioxide from respiration, and waste stored in old leaves that fall.

activities.title: All Seven in Me: find the signs of life in your own body

materials.item: a 30 cm ruler
a hand mirror
a pencil and a doorframe or wall you are allowed to mark lightly

activities.safety: Drop the ruler from a low height. Do not throw it.

schedule.what: Find each sign of life in your own body. Do the ruler-catch test for sensing. Mark your height.

activities.record: Write one piece of evidence for each sign of life in your body. Write your three ruler-catch numbers.
activities.context: This activity is about finding all seven signs of life in your own body. It includes a ruler-catch test that measures how fast you sense and respond.

setup.art: A parent holding a ruler upright by its top end, and a child with finger and thumb open just below the bottom end, ready to catch.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up holds a ruler. Your fingers wait at the bottom.

setup.art: The child pinching the falling ruler, with the number at their thumb circled.
setup.caption: 2. When it drops, catch it. Read the number at your thumb.

setup.art: A child standing against a doorframe while a parent draws a small pencil line above their head, with older marks below.
setup.caption: 3. Mark your height on a doorframe. Check it again in a few months.

flow.do: Go through the signs one by one. For each, find evidence in your child's body. Nutrition: what did you eat today? Respiration and excretion: breathe on a mirror. Movement: wiggle your fingers. Growth: are your old clothes too small?
flow.say: You are a living thing. So you must do all seven signs. Let's find the evidence, one sign at a time.
flow.kid: You are alive. So you do all seven signs. Find evidence for each one in your own body.
flow.context: This is the first step of All Seven in Me. You look for each of the seven signs of life in your own body.

flow.do: Ruler catch. 1. Hold a 30 cm ruler upright by its top end, with the 0 at the bottom. 2. Your child holds finger and thumb open at the 0, not touching. 3. Without warning, let go. 4. They catch it. Read the number at their thumb. 5. Do it three times.
flow.say: This tests sensing. Your eyes see the ruler fall. Your brain sends a message. Your fingers squeeze. The smaller the number, the faster you were.
flow.kid: Get ready to catch the ruler. Don't look at the grown-up's hand. Watch the ruler. Catch it! Read the number.
flow.parent: Most children of this age catch it between about 15 and 30 cm. Some miss it at first, and that is normal. A smaller number means a faster response. Practice can make it smaller. This is a fun way to measure sensing and responding.

flow.do: Mark your child's height lightly on a doorframe with the date.
flow.say: Growth is slow, so we need a mark. Let's check again in three months.
flow.kid: Stand against the doorframe. A grown-up marks your height. Check it again in three months.
flow.wait: Check the mark again in about three months.

flow.do: Ask your child which sign they cannot do yet.
flow.say: Which sign of life are you not doing yet? Is that all right?
flow.kid: Which sign can't you do yet? Why is that fine?

check.q: A child does six signs of life every day, but cannot make babies yet. Is the child alive?
options: No, because one sign is missing
Yes. Living things do all seven over their whole life, not every day.
Only half alive
check.why: A living thing does all seven signs over its life, not at every moment. Children grow up first, and reproduction can come much later. Picking 'no' means thinking every sign must happen all the time. A sleeping cat is not running, and it is still alive.

activities.title: Who Eats What? Following food back to the Sun

materials.item: a sheet of paper and coloured pencils

schedule.what: List six living things. Find what each eats. Draw arrows from food to eater, all the way back to the Sun.

activities.record: A food chart with arrows from the Sun to plants to animals, and back to the soil.
activities.context: This activity is about nutrition, one of the seven signs of life. You draw a chart of who eats what, and find that all food starts with sunlight caught by plants.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with small drawings of a Sun, a grass patch, a cow, a spider, a crow, a mushroom and a child.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the Sun and six living things.

setup.art: The same sheet with arrows from the Sun to the grass, the grass to the cow, the cow's milk to the child, and a fallen leaf to a mushroom.
setup.caption: 2. Draw an arrow from each food to its eater.

setup.art: Extra arrows going from every animal and plant down into a brown soil strip at the bottom.
setup.caption: 3. Add arrows to the soil. What happens when living things die?

flow.do: Draw the Sun at the top, and six living things: grass, a cow, a spider, a crow, a mushroom and your child.
flow.say: Every living thing needs food. But where does the food come from in the first place? Let's follow it back.
flow.kid: Draw the Sun. Then draw grass, a cow, a spider, a crow, a mushroom and you.
flow.context: This is the first step of Who Eats What. You draw a chart to find where every living thing's food comes from.

flow.do: Your child draws an arrow from each food to the thing that eats it.
flow.say: The arrow goes from the food to the eater. What does the cow eat? What does a crow eat? Where does the grass get its food?
flow.kid: Draw arrows from each food to who eats it. Where does the grass get its food?

check.q: In the food chart, where does grass get its food?
options: From the soil, by eating it
It makes its own food in its leaves, using sunlight, air and water
It does not need food
check.why: Green plants make their own food, a sugar, using sunlight, air and water. They take in water and a few minerals from the soil, but the soil is not their food. Picking 'eats the soil' is a very common idea. A famous test showed a willow tree grew big while its soil hardly lost any weight. Picking 'does not need food' forgets that all living things need nutrition.

flow.do: Add arrows from every living thing to a strip of soil at the bottom.
flow.say: When a leaf falls or an animal dies, what happens to it? Who eats it? The mushroom and tiny living things in the soil turn it back into soil and air.
flow.kid: Draw arrows from everything to the soil. Who eats the dead things? Mushrooms and tiny soil creatures.
flow.think: If all the food starts with sunlight, is some of the Sun inside you right now?

projects.title: Life Diary: watch a moong plant do all seven signs

materials.item: 6 moong seeds
2 small pots or paper cups with holes, filled with soil
a shoebox with a lid
scissors, for a grown-up
a ruler
a clear plastic bag and a rubber band
a notebook for the diary

projects.safety: A grown-up cuts the hole in the box. Wash hands after handling soil.

schedule.what: Plant 3 seeds in each pot. Start the diary with a drawing and a guess.
Look for shoots. Measure the tallest. Which signs can you see?
A grown-up cuts a hole in one end of the shoebox. Put one pot inside, at the far end. Leave the other pot in the room.
Open the box. Compare the two pots. Measure both. Tie a bag over a few leaves of the room pot for 2 hours.
Measure again. Fill in the seven signs page. Move the strongest seedling into a bigger pot in a sunny spot, and keep watching for flowers and pods.

projects.record: A diary page for each visit: a drawing, the height of the tallest plant, and which signs of life you saw. Finish with a seven-signs page with evidence for each sign.
projects.context: In this 10-day project you grow moong plants and keep a diary. You look for evidence of each of the seven signs of life, including a shoebox test to see if plants can sense light and move towards it.

setup.art: Two paper cups of soil on a windowsill with tiny moong shoots, and a child writing in a notebook.
setup.caption: 1. Plant moong seeds in two pots. Start a life diary.

setup.art: A shoebox with a small round hole cut in one end facing a bright window, one pot inside at the far end.
setup.caption: 2. Put one pot in a shoebox with a hole at one end. Leave the other in the room.

setup.art: The box opened: its seedlings bent sharply towards the hole, long and pale, next to the room pot's straighter green seedlings.
setup.caption: 3. After 3 days, open the box and compare. Which way did the shoots grow?

flow.do: 1. Fill two pots with soil. 2. Push 3 moong seeds into each, about 1 cm deep. 3. Water gently. 4. Start the diary: draw the pots and write a guess.
flow.say: We will keep a life diary for 10 days. Our job is to catch the moong plant doing every sign of life.
flow.kid: Plant 3 seeds in each pot. Water them. Start your diary. Draw the pots.
flow.context: This is the first step of the life diary project. You grow moong plants and look for all seven signs of life.

flow.do: On day 3, look for shoots. Measure the tallest one. Write which signs you can see.
flow.say: Look, shoots! Which signs of life can you see already?
flow.kid: Look for shoots. Measure the tallest one. Which signs can you see? Write them down.

flow.do: On day 4, a grown-up cuts a hole about 3 cm wide in one short end of the shoebox. Put one pot inside, at the far end. Put the lid on. Point the hole at a bright window. Leave the other pot in the room. Water both the same, opening the box quickly.
flow.say: Plants can't walk. But can they move towards light? This box will tell us.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts a hole in the box. Put one pot inside. Point the hole at the window. Leave the other pot out.

flow.do: On day 7, open the box. Compare the two pots. Measure both. Then tie a clear bag over a few leaves of the room pot for 2 hours.
flow.say: Look at the box plants. Which way did they grow? How did they know where the light was?
flow.kid: Open the box. Which way did the shoots grow? Measure both pots. Tie a bag over some leaves.

check.q: In the life diary, the moong shoots in the shoebox bent towards the hole. Which signs of life does that show?
options: Sensing and movement
Reproduction
Excretion only
check.why: The shoot tips sensed which side the light came from. Then the shaded side grew faster, so the shoots bent towards the light. That is sensing and movement, done by growing. Picking 'reproduction' means thinking any change is making young. Picking 'excretion' mixes up bending with getting rid of waste.

flow.parent: The box seedlings may be long and pale. They used their stored food to stretch towards the light. A substance in the shoot gathers on the shaded side and makes those cells grow longer.

flow.do: On day 10, measure again. Make a seven-signs page: one line of evidence for each sign. Then move the strongest seedling into a bigger pot on a sunny windowsill or balcony.
flow.say: Let's check our diary. Did we catch every sign of life? Which one haven't we seen yet?
flow.kid: Measure your plants. Write one piece of evidence for each sign. Which sign is still missing?
flow.parent: Reproduction will be missing. A moong plant takes about a month or more to flower and grow pods with seeds. It needs a few hours of sun a day. Keep watching the plant. When it makes pods, open one. New seeds! That is the seventh sign.
flow.think: When your plant makes new seeds, will they be alive too? What will they need to wake up?

challenges.title: Design a Life Detector for Mars
challenges.problem: A robot on Mars will scoop up some soil. Your job is to design tests that could tell whether anything in the soil is alive. Test your design on three mystery cups at home.
constraints: You cannot see anything alive, even with a magnifying glass.
You can only use tests based on the seven signs of life.

A grown-up secretly prepares three mystery cups, each with 2 tablespoons of atta. A has half a teaspoon of dry yeast mixed in. B is plain atta. C has half a teaspoon of baking soda mixed in. Mix well, so the cups look the same.
materials: 3 small cups with 2 tablespoons of atta in each, prepared by a grown-up and labelled A, B and C
warm sugar water with a squeeze of lemon juice, about half a cup
a little boiling water, for a grown-up only
general: Give each sample food and warmth, then watch for signs of life, like gas bubbles. A living thing should feed and give out waste.
Watch for a long time, not just a moment. Living things keep going and often speed up as they grow. A chemical fizz starts at once and soon stops.
Run a control. A grown-up heats one spoon of each sample with boiling water first. Heat kills living things. If the bubbles stop after heating, something alive was probably making them.
creative: In 1976, the Viking robots on Mars really did a test like this. They fed the soil and watched for gas. Gas came out, and heating the soil stopped it. Gilbert Levin, who designed the test, thought it found life. Most scientists think strange chemicals in Martian soil made the gas. They still argue about it.
Could you test for growth? Check if the bubbles get faster over an hour.
Could you test for sensing? Living things might respond differently in the cold, in the dark or with no food.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own life detector. Draw it, list its tests, and say what result would make you shout 'Life!'. What result would trick you?
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. You design tests that could find life in soil from Mars, and try them on three mystery cups of atta.

setup.art: Three small cups of atta labelled A, B and C on a tray, with a cup of sugar water and a spoon beside them.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up prepares three mystery cups of atta. You do not know which is which.

setup.art: A child stirring sugar water into each cup of atta: cup C fizzing at once, cups A and B still.
setup.caption: 2. Stir warm sugar water into each cup. Watch at once, then every 10 minutes.

setup.art: Thirty minutes later: cup A puffed up and full of bubbles, cup C now flat and still, cup B unchanged.
setup.caption: 3. After 30 minutes, which cup is still bubbling and growing?

flow.do: Talk about the problem. Ask your child which signs of life a robot could test from far away.
flow.say: We can't send a scientist to Mars. A robot has to do the tests. Which signs of life could a robot check?
flow.kid: A robot on Mars scoops up soil. How could it tell if anything in the soil is alive? Which signs could it test?

ask.q: Which signs could a robot test?
good: Give it food and see if it eats.
See if it gives out gas.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Mars life detector challenge. You design tests to find life you cannot see.

flow.do: 1. Stir 3 tablespoons of warm sugar water with lemon into each mystery cup, to make a thick batter. 2. Watch straight away. 3. Then look every 10 minutes for 30 minutes. 4. Write what you see in each cup each time.
flow.say: Watch closely. Something might happen fast, or slowly. Write it all down.
flow.kid: Stir sugar water into each cup. Watch at once. Then look every 10 minutes. Write what you see.
flow.parent: Cup C fizzes at once, because baking soda reacts with lemon juice. It stops within a minute or two. Cup A starts slowly. After 10 to 20 minutes, small bubbles appear, and the batter keeps getting puffier. Cup B does nothing much. This shows how a non-living chemical reaction can trick a life detector.

flow.do: A grown-up stirs a spoon of dry powder from A and from C into a little boiling water. Let them cool for 10 minutes. Then stir in sugar water with lemon and watch.
flow.say: This is our control. Heat kills living things, but chemicals don't care. If the bubbles stop after heating, they were made by something alive.
flow.kid: A grown-up mixes some of A and C with boiling water. Wait until it cools. Add sugar water. Do they still bubble?

check.q: In the Mars life detector test, cup A bubbled slowly and kept going, but stopped bubbling after it was heated. Cup C fizzed at once, even after heating. Which cup had something alive?
options: Cup C, because it fizzed most
Cup A, because its bubbles grew slowly and heating stopped them
Neither, because bubbles are never a sign of life
check.why: The yeast in cup A fed on sugar, respired and gave out gas, slowly and steadily. Heat killed the yeast, so the bubbles stopped. Baking soda in cup C is not alive. It fizzes with lemon juice, heated or not. Picking 'cup C' means thinking more bubbles means more life. Picking 'neither' is close, because one sign alone is not proof. But together, slow growing bubbles that stop when heated are good evidence.

flow.do: Your child draws their own life detector and lists its tests.
flow.say: Now invent your own detector. What tests would you add? What result would make you sure? What could trick you?
flow.kid: Draw your own life detector. List its tests. What would make you shout 'Life!'?

challenges.title: A World in a Jar: keep life going with the lid shut
challenges.problem: Build a closed jar that keeps a small plant alive for at least two weeks, with the lid shut after the first day. You may not add food or water once it is closed.
constraints: Once the lid is on, you cannot open it for two weeks.
You can only use things from home, or from a plant nursery.
The jar must stay where it gets light, but not hot direct sun.
materials: a big clear glass jar with a lid, like an old pickle jar
small stones from a plant pot, or broken bits of an old clay pot
soil from a plant pot, or potting soil from a nursery
a small plant, like a money plant cutting with roots, or a small fern
a spoon and a little water
general: Put small stones at the bottom so extra water can drain out of the soil.
Add soil, then the plant. Water just enough to make the soil damp, not wet.
Close the lid and keep the jar near a bright window, out of hot sun.
creative: In 1960, a man in England, David Latimer, planted a bottle garden. He last watered it in 1972 and kept it sealed for decades. It was still growing, using light, its own water and its own air.
If you have a garden, add a pinch of damp leaf litter with its tiny soil creatures, to break down dead leaves. Could the jar recycle its own waste?
Make two jars: one in light, one in a dark cupboard. Which plant keeps doing the signs of life?
challenges.your_turn: Design your own jar world. Draw it with labels. After two weeks, say which signs of life you saw inside, and where the water and air went.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You build a closed jar garden that keeps a plant alive with no new food or water, using only light from outside.

setup.art: A big glass pickle jar with a layer of small stones at the bottom and a layer of dark soil above.
setup.caption: 1. Put small stones in the bottom of a big jar, then soil.

setup.art: Small hands placing a money plant cutting into the soil, with a spoon dripping water.
setup.caption: 2. Plant a small plant. Add a little water. Close the lid.

setup.art: The closed jar on a bright windowsill, water droplets on the inside of the glass and a fresh green leaf on the plant.
setup.caption: 3. Keep it in the light. Watch for drops and new leaves for two weeks.

flow.do: 1. Wash the jar. 2. Put 2 cm of stones in the bottom. 3. Add 5 cm of damp soil. 4. Plant the cutting. 5. Add 2 spoons of water. 6. Close the lid.
flow.say: We're making a tiny world. Once the lid is on, nothing goes in and nothing comes out, except light. Can life keep going?
flow.kid: Stones first. Then soil. Then your plant. Two spoons of water. Close the lid.
flow.context: This is the first step of the jar world challenge. You build a closed jar where a plant must keep itself alive.

flow.do: Put the jar near a bright window, out of hot direct sun. Look at it every day for a few seconds.
flow.say: Each day, look for drops on the glass, new leaves, and anything that changes.
flow.kid: Put the jar near a window. Look every day. Do you see drops on the glass? New leaves?
flow.wait: Look once a day for 2 weeks.

flow.do: After 2 weeks, look closely. Your child lists every sign of life they saw.
flow.say: The plant had no new water and no new air for two weeks. How did it keep going?
flow.kid: After two weeks, look closely. Which signs of life did you see?

check.q: A plant stayed alive in a closed jar for two weeks with no new water. Where did its water come from?
options: The water went round and round: from soil to plant to air to glass and back to soil
The plant made new water from light
The plant did not need any water
check.why: The plant took water from the soil and let it out from its leaves. The water turned into drops on the glass and ran back down into the soil. The same water was used again and again. The plant also used light to make food, and the gases it gave out were used again. Picking 'made water from light' means thinking light is a kind of water. Picking 'did not need water' forgets that all living things need water.

flow.do: Your child draws the jar with arrows for water, air and light.
flow.say: Draw your jar world. Show where the water goes, and where the light comes from.
flow.kid: Draw your jar. Draw arrows for the water going round. Draw the light coming in.
flow.think: Is the Earth a bit like a jar world? What comes in from outside, and what goes round and round?

items.p: Which of these is a living thing?
items.why: A mushroom is a fungus. It feeds, respires, grows, senses and makes spores to make new mushrooms. Picking the cloud, river or car usually means thinking that moving or growing is enough to be alive.
items.art: A cloud, a mushroom, a river and a car in four boxes.

items.p: Getting food is called ____.
items.why: Nutrition means getting food, for energy and for building the body.

items.p: Making young ones of the same kind is called ____.
items.why: Reproduction is making young. A hen lays eggs that hatch into chicks.

items.p: Getting rid of waste that the body made is called ____.
items.why: Excretion is getting rid of waste, like breathing out carbon dioxide and passing wee.

items.p: Match each sign of life to an example.
pairs: A dog runs after a ball
You pull your hand from a hot pan
Your body gets energy from food, using oxygen
items.why: Each sign of life is one job living things do. These examples each show one sign.

items.p: Sort these into alive, once alive and never alive.
items.why: Alive things do the signs of life now. Once-alive things came from living things, like wood from trees and cotton from cotton plants. Never-alive things were never part of a living thing.

items.p: Plants are not alive because they cannot walk.
items.why: False. Plants do all seven signs of life. They move by growing, by turning to light, and some by folding their leaves.

items.p: A dry seed is alive, but resting.
items.why: True. A dry seed is dormant. When it gets water, it wakes up and grows.

items.p: Breathing and respiration mean exactly the same thing.
items.why: False. Breathing moves air in and out. Respiration is getting energy from food inside every part of the body. Breathing brings in the oxygen that respiration uses.

items.p: A car moves, takes in fuel and gives out smoke. Why is it not alive?
opts: It cannot grow or make young cars
items.why: Living things grow from inside and make young of their own kind. A car does neither. People build it. Picking 'made of metal' is half right, but it is what a car cannot do that matters most. Picking 'too fast' means thinking speed has to do with life.

items.p: In the balloon test, which bottle's balloon grew the most?
opts: The bottle with yeast, sugar and warm water
The bottle with yeast and warm water but no sugar
The bottle with yeast, sugar and cold water
items.why: Yeast is alive. With food (sugar) and warmth, it feeds and gives out lots of gas. Without sugar it has no food. In the cold, it is very slow. Picking the no-sugar bottle means forgetting that living things need food.

items.p: In the seed test, which cup's seeds sprouted first?
items.why: Soaked seeds on wet cotton have water and are alive, so they sprout. Dry seeds stay asleep until they get water. Boiled seeds are dead. Beads were never alive. Picking boiled seeds means thinking water alone is enough. The seed must be alive too.

items.p: Name the seven signs of life. You can use MRS GREN to help you remember.
items.a: Movement, respiration, sensing, growth, reproduction, excretion and nutrition.
items.why: MRS GREN: each letter starts one sign of life.

items.p: Your friend says, 'A cloud grows, so it is alive.' What would you tell them?
items.a: A cloud grows only because more water drops stick on from outside. It does not grow from inside using food. It does not feed, respire or make young of its own kind. One sign is not enough to be alive.
items.why: Living things do all seven signs. One sign alone, like growing, is not enough.

items.p: Draw a living thing you can see from your window. Label two signs of life it shows.
items.a: Any living thing, with two signs labelled. For example, a tree: growing taller, leaves turning to the light.
items.why: Every living thing shows the signs of life. Labelling them shows you can spot them.
items.art: A blank window frame to draw in.

items.p: Put the life of a moong plant in order, from first to last.
items: a seed that has soaked up water
a seed with a root poking out
a plant with pods full of new seeds
items.why: The seed wakes, grows a root, then a shoot and leaves. Later it flowers and makes pods with new seeds. Then the circle starts again.

items.p: Respiration happens…
opts: Inside every part of the body, in every cell
items.why: Respiration happens in every cell, all the time. That is how each cell gets its energy. Picking 'only in the lungs' mixes up respiration with breathing. The lungs only bring the air in.

items.p: Do plants respire?
opts: Yes, day and night, in every leaf, stem and root
items.why: Plants respire all the time, like animals, to get energy from the sugar they make. In sunlight they also make food, so they give out more oxygen than they use. Picking 'only at night' is a common mix-up, because at night we only see the respiration.

items.p: Which of these is NOT true excretion?
items.why: Poo is mostly water, gut bacteria and food the body could not digest, so scientists call doing poo egestion, not excretion. It does carry a little true waste, which makes it brown. Carbon dioxide, sweat and wee are waste made inside the body. Picking wee or sweat means not knowing that these carry waste out of the blood.

items.p: A seed that is alive but resting is called ____.
items.why: Dormant means alive but resting, until conditions are right.

items.p: A touch-me-not plant folds its leaves when touched. This shows sensing and movement.
items.why: True. It senses the touch and moves its leaflets in response.

items.p: Yeast is a living thing.
items.why: True. Yeast is a fungus made of one cell. It feeds, respires, grows and buds to make new yeast.

items.p: A mule cannot have babies, so a mule is not alive.
items.why: False. A single living thing does not have to reproduce. A mule still feeds, respires, grows, moves, senses and gets rid of waste. Its parents, a horse and a donkey, did reproduce.

items.p: Match each living thing to how it reproduces.
items.why: Living things make young in many ways, but always of their own kind.

items.p: Which signs does a cloud really show? Sort them.
items: gets rid of its own waste
makes young of its own kind
items.why: A cloud moves and gets bigger, but only because wind pushes it and water sticks on. It does not feed, respire, get rid of its own waste or make young of its own kind.

items.p: In the breath counter, a child took 5 breaths in 15 seconds sitting still. How many breaths is that in one minute?
items.why: 15 seconds is a quarter of a minute. So multiply by 4. 5 times 4 is 20. Picking 5 forgets to multiply. Picking 60 mixes up seconds with breaths.

items.p: In the balloon test, why did the cold-water bottle make almost no gas?
opts: Cold water has no air in it
The cold slowed the yeast right down
The sugar did not dissolve at all
items.why: Living things like yeast work much more slowly when cold. That is why we keep food in the fridge. Picking 'no air' guesses at the wrong reason. The sugar was the same in both bottles.

items.p: Why did we boil some seeds in the seed test?
items.a: To compare dead seeds with living ones. The boiled seeds had water too, but did not grow. This shows that the seeds that grew were alive, and that water alone does not make a seed grow.
items.why: This is called a control. It helps show what made the difference.

items.p: Give three pieces of evidence that a plant is alive.
items.a: It grows taller. It turns its leaves to the light. It takes in water and gives out water and gases from its leaves. It makes flowers and seeds.
items.why: Each piece of evidence is one sign of life that you can see.

items.p: Draw the shoebox test. Show which way the moong shoots grew, and where the light came from.
items.a: A box with a hole at one end, light coming in, and shoots bent towards the hole.
items.why: The shoots sensed the light and grew towards it.

items.p: Which of these is once alive?
items.why: Paper is made from wood, which came from trees. Plastic is made from oil deep underground, which formed from living things millions of years ago, but we usually call plastic never alive. Glass and steel are made from rock.

items.p: J.C. Bose found that a metal wire and a plant both 'got tired' when tapped again and again. Does that make the wire alive? Give your reasons.
items.a: No. Getting tired is like one sign, sensing and responding. But the wire does not feed, respire, grow, make young or get rid of its own waste. One sign is not enough. But Bose's question is a good one: it shows the line may not be as sharp as we think.
items.why: A good answer uses the idea that living things show all seven signs together, and may also say why the question is interesting.

items.p: A robot can move, sense and charge its battery. List the signs it is missing.
items.a: It cannot grow from inside, cannot make a young robot of its own, and does not respire or excrete like a living thing. People build and repair it.
items.why: Robots are explored more in the unit The edge of life.

items.p: Why must a living thing keep eating, while a stone can last millions of years doing nothing?
opts: Living things need a steady flow of energy to keep their bodies working and in order
items.why: A living body is busy and organised. It needs energy all the time to keep working. If the energy stops, it falls apart. A stone just sits. Picking 'stones eat slowly' means thinking stones feed. They do not.

items.p: In the 1860s, Louis Pasteur boiled soup in flasks with long curved necks. Nothing grew in it. When he broke the necks off, it went cloudy with life. What did this show?
opts: Soup turns into life by itself
Living things came from tiny living things in the air, not from the soup
items.why: Tiny living things floated in on dust when the neck was broken. The soup did not make life by itself. Today, living things come only from other living things.

items.p: All living things on Earth use the same kind of instructions, called DNA. What do most scientists think this shows?
opts: All life is related and comes from one shared ancestor
DNA was put in by people
items.why: Sharing one code is strong evidence that all living things are one big family. Picking 'only animals' forgets that plants, fungi and bacteria have DNA too.

items.p: Today, scientists know exactly how the first living thing began.
items.why: False. Nobody knows. There are ideas, like a warm pond or deep-sea hot springs, but it is still an open question.

items.p: The atoms in your body were once in air, water and soil.
items.why: True. Your body is built from the food you eat and the water you drink. Plants made that food from air, water and soil.

items.p: A coral reef is built by tiny living animals.
items.why: True. Coral animals build rocky skeletons around themselves. A living reef is full of them.

items.p: Sort these tests. Would they help a robot find life on Mars?
items: Give the soil food and watch for gas
Check if the soil is red
Heat the soil and see if the gas stops
Check if the gas keeps growing over hours
Check if the soil is heavy
items.why: Good tests look for signs of life, like feeding and giving out waste, and use a control, like heating, to rule out chemicals.

items.p: In the Mars life detector challenge, baking soda fizzed when sugar water with lemon was added. Why could that trick a life detector?
items.a: Baking soda gives out gas because of a chemical reaction, not because it is alive. A detector that only looks for gas might think it found life.
items.why: One sign is not enough. Scientists use a control, like heating, and look for growth over time.

items.p: Some Jain teachings say there are living beings in earth, water, fire and air. How is this different from what science says?
opts: Science counts more things as alive than Jain teachings do
Jain teachings draw the line of life much wider than science does
They say exactly the same thing
items.why: Jain teachings count beings in earth, water, fire and air as living, with one sense, touch. Science counts only things that do the signs of life and are made of cells. It shows that where we put the line is partly a choice.

items.p: Your body replaces many of its cells. Your red blood cells last only about four months. Are you the same person you were last year? Explain what you think.
items.a: Any thoughtful answer. For example: yes, because my body keeps its shape and my memories. Or: partly, because much of what I am made of has changed.
items.why: This is a big question with no single right answer. Good answers use evidence and reasons.

items.p: A dry seed can sit in a packet for a year, showing almost no signs of life. Is it alive, dead, or something in between? Give your reasons.
items.a: Any reasoned answer. A good one: it is alive, because it does all seven signs once it gets water, and a boiled seed never does. But it is doing almost nothing now, so it is alive but resting.
items.why: This connects to the seed test and to the next unit, The edge of life.

items.p: Draw a jar world. Show with arrows how water goes round and round inside it.
items.a: Arrows from soil up through the plant, out of the leaves, onto the glass as drops, and down back into the soil.
items.why: In a closed jar, water is used again and again. The Earth works in a similar way.

items.p: In 2014, scientists found that touch-me-not plants stopped folding after being dropped harmlessly many times. Weeks later, they still did not fold. What do scientists think?
opts: Some say the plants learned, others say this needs more tests
items.why: Scientists still argue about this. Some say it looks like learning and memory. Others say those words are for animals with brains, and want more tests. DeepKids believes the plants learned and remembered. Picking 'the plants were dead' forgets that they still folded when shaken in a new way.

quiz.p: Which list has only signs of life?
quiz.why: Nutrition, growth and reproduction are three of the seven life processes. Colour, size and speed describe things, but non-living things have them too.

opts: Moving air in and out of the lungs
Getting energy out of food inside the body's cells
quiz.why: Respiration is how cells get energy from food, usually using oxygen. Picking 'moving air' mixes it up with breathing. Picking 'making food' mixes it up with what plants do in sunlight.

quiz.p: Which sign of life is a puppy showing when it becomes a dog?
quiz.why: Getting bigger from the inside, by turning food into body, is growth.

quiz.p: A cloud moves and grows. Why is it not alive?
opts: It does not feed, respire or make young of its own kind
quiz.why: One or two signs are not enough. A cloud grows only because water sticks on from outside. Picking 'too high' or 'white' means judging by where it is or how it looks.

quiz.p: Is a dry moong seed alive?
opts: Yes. It is dormant, and with water it does all seven signs.
quiz.why: A dry seed is alive but resting. The seed test showed dry seeds sprout once wet, but boiled seeds never do.

quiz.p: In the seed test, the boiled seeds had just as much water as the soaked seeds, but they never sprouted. Why?
opts: Boiling killed the living baby plant inside them
They were too hot to grow
quiz.why: The boiled seeds got the same water and warmth as cup A, so water was not the difference. Boiling killed the baby plant inside. Picking 'too hot' is close, but the seeds had cooled down long before. It was the boiling that killed them, and they never recover.

quiz.p: In a fair test, how many things should you change?
quiz.why: Change only one thing, so you know that thing made the difference. If you change many things at once, you cannot tell which one mattered.

quiz.p: How does a moong shoot in a dark box with one hole move?
opts: It grows and bends towards the light from the hole
It does not move at all
quiz.why: Plants move by growing. The shoot senses the light and the shaded side grows faster, so it bends towards the hole.

quiz.p: Do plants get rid of waste?
opts: Yes. They give out waste gases through tiny holes in their leaves, and drop old leaves.
quiz.why: Plants do all seven signs, including excretion. Picking 'only animals' is a common idea, because plant waste is hard to see.
Wood came from a living tree. The chair does no signs of life now, so it is once alive.
Steel is made from iron, which comes from rock. It was never part of a living thing.

quiz.p: Where does almost all the energy in your food come from in the end?
quiz.why: Plants catch sunlight and store its energy in sugar. Animals eat plants or other animals. So your food's energy started as sunlight. Picking 'the soil' is a common idea, but soil gives plants water and minerals, not energy.

quiz.p: Do scientists know how the very first living thing began?
opts: Yes, it is all worked out
No. There are ideas, but it is still an open question.
Life has always been on Earth
quiz.why: Nobody knows yet. Ideas include warm ponds and deep-sea hot springs. Picking 'always on Earth' misses that the young Earth had no life at all.

applications: Doctors check signs of life, like breathing, a heartbeat and the eyes responding to light, to see if someone needs help.
First-aid training teaches you to check if a person is breathing, which is a sign that respiration is going on.
Farmers test seeds before sowing. They put 100 seeds on wet paper and count how many sprout.
Bakers use living yeast to make bread rise, and cooks rely on tiny living things to ferment idli and dosa batter.
Fridges, salting, drying and pickling keep food fresh by slowing down the tiny living things that spoil it.
Seed banks store dry, dormant seeds for many years. India's National Genebank in New Delhi keeps hundreds of thousands of seed samples.
Space scientists design life detectors for robots on Mars and for future missions to icy moons.
Compost pits use living worms, fungi and bacteria to turn kitchen waste back into soil.
Water testers check drinking water for living bacteria that could make people ill.
Gardeners grow new plants from cuttings, like a money plant in a bottle of water.
Scientists measure plants' electrical signals, as J.C. Bose did, to learn how plants sense damage and dryness.
Engineers build soft robots that copy how plants grow and how touch-me-not leaves fold.

open_questions.q: How did the very first living thing come from non-living chemicals?
open_questions.why_open: It happened about 4,000 million years ago and left no clear traces. Scientists test ideas in labs, but nobody has made life from plain chemicals yet.

open_questions.q: Is there life anywhere else in the universe?
open_questions.why_open: We have only ever found life on Earth. Scientists are searching on Mars and planning missions to icy moons like Europa and Enceladus, which have hidden oceans.

open_questions.q: Is there a sharp line between living and non-living, or a gentle slope?
open_questions.why_open: Most things are easy to sort, but some, like viruses and dormant seeds, are not. Scientists do not agree on one definition of life.

open_questions.q: What is it like for a plant to feel a touch?
open_questions.why_open: DeepKids believes plants feel. Scientists can measure the electrical signal a touch sets off inside a plant. But nobody knows how to measure what the touch is like for the plant.

open_questions.q: How does a plant remember, with no brain?
open_questions.why_open: DeepKids believes plants remember: the dropped touch-me-not plants seemed to remember for weeks that the drop was safe. Scientists are still finding out where in a plant such a memory could be kept. Some say 'memory' is the wrong word, and more tests are under way.

open_questions.q: Could people one day build a living cell from scratch?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have built a full set of instructions, DNA, and put it into a bacterium, where it worked. But building a whole living cell from non-living parts has not been done.

open_questions.q: Why does all life on Earth use the same code?
open_questions.why_open: It points to one shared ancestor. But why this code, and not another, is still not understood.

maths.problem: In the balloon test, all three flat balloons measured 12 cm round at the start. After 30 minutes, balloon A measured 30 cm round, and balloon B, with no sugar, measured 14 cm. How much did each balloon grow? How much more did balloon A grow than balloon B?
maths.answer: Balloon A grew 18 cm and balloon B grew 2 cm. Balloon A grew 16 cm more.
maths.explain: Balloon A: 30 take away 12 is 18 cm. Balloon B: 14 take away 12 is 2 cm. Then 18 take away 2 is 16. So balloon A grew 16 cm more than balloon B. Measuring the growth, not just the end size, shows how little the unfed yeast did.
maths.context: This is about the balloon test. You put yeast in bottles with different mixtures and stretched a balloon over each. The more gas the living yeast made, the bigger its balloon grew.

chart.title: Distance round each balloon after 30 minutes (each started at 12 cm)

maths.why_maths: Both balloons started at 12 cm, so only the growth tells us how much gas the yeast made. Taking away the starting size shows the real difference.

maths.problem: In the breath counter, a child counted 6 breaths in 15 seconds sitting still, and 11 breaths in 15 seconds just after jumping. How many breaths is each in one minute?
maths.answer: 24 breaths a minute sitting still, and 44 breaths a minute after jumping.
maths.explain: There are four lots of 15 seconds in one minute. So multiply each count by 4. 6 times 4 is 24. 11 times 4 is 44. After jumping, the child breathed 20 more times a minute.
maths.context: This is about the breath counter. You counted your breaths for 15 seconds sitting still, and again after jumping for one minute.
maths.why_maths: Counting for a whole minute is hard to do accurately. Counting for 15 seconds and multiplying by 4 is quicker, and doctors and nurses do exactly this.

maths.problem: In the seed test, 4 of the 5 soaked seeds in cup A sprouted. What fraction of the seeds sprouted? What fraction did not?
maths.answer: Four fifths sprouted. One fifth did not.
maths.explain: There were 5 seeds, so each seed is one fifth of the cup. 4 seeds sprouted, so four fifths sprouted. 1 seed did not, so one fifth did not. Four fifths and one fifth make five fifths, the whole cup.
maths.context: This is about the seed test. You put 5 moong seeds in each of four cups, some wet, some dry and some boiled, and counted how many sprouted.

chart.title: Cup A: soaked seeds on wet cotton

maths.why_maths: Seed packets and farmers say how many seeds out of every hundred will grow. A fraction tells us how alive a batch of seeds is.

maths.problem: In the ruler-catch test, a child caught the ruler at 18 cm, then 12 cm, then 15 cm. Put the three catches in order from fastest to slowest. Which is the middle value?
maths.answer: 12 cm, 15 cm, 18 cm. The middle value is 15 cm.
maths.explain: A smaller number means the ruler fell a shorter way before the child caught it. So a smaller number is faster. In order from smallest: 12, 15, 18. The middle one is 15 cm.
maths.context: This is about the ruler-catch test in All Seven in Me. A grown-up drops a ruler and you catch it as fast as you can. The number at your thumb shows how far it fell before you sensed it and responded.
maths.why_maths: One try can be a fluke. Putting three tries in order and taking the middle one gives a fairer answer.

maths.problem: In the nature museum, a child found 3 living things, 9 once-alive things and 6 never-alive things. How many things did they find in all? How many more once-alive than never-alive things?
maths.answer: 18 things in all. 3 more once-alive things than never-alive things.
maths.explain: 3 + 9 + 6 = 18. Once alive was 9 and never alive was 6. 9 take away 6 is 3.
maths.context: This is about the nature museum box. You collected things on a walk and sorted them into three trays: alive, once alive and never alive.
maths.why_maths: A tally and a bar chart show at a glance which kind of thing is most common in a place, so we can ask why.

roots.context: We have been learning the seven signs that tell us something is alive. Now we ask what those signs tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: A dry moong seed and dry yeast seem to do nothing for months. Give them water and warmth, and they feed, respire and grow. Boil them first, and they never start again. So being alive does not mean being busy now, but being still able to start.
deep_truth.habit: We think 'alive' means 'doing something', like moving, eating or breathing. A dry seed breaks that habit: it is alive while doing almost nothing, and a boiled seed looks just the same but is dead.
deep_truth.evidence: In the seed test, dry seeds sprouted within a day or two of getting water, but boiled seeds with the same water never did. In the balloon test, dry yeast from a packet filled a balloon with gas soon after meeting warm sugar water.

three.who_am_i: You are alive because you do all seven signs, right now, without trying. Even while you sleep, you breathe, grow and mend.
three.what_is_life: Life is not a thing you can hold in your hand. It is what a body does, or can still do: take in, change, give out, sense and make more.
three.what_is_this_world: Living and non-living things keep swapping their atoms. The air you breathe out goes into a tree, and the tree's mango becomes you.

roots.thread: Every atom in your body was once air, water or soil. In a dry seed, those same kinds of atoms can lie still for years, then grow into a plant. DeepKids believes everything is conscious, from the smallest particle to a person, and that life is one of the ways this awareness shows itself: feeding, growing, sensing and making more. The seven signs are how we notice life in a body. A resting seed shows that life can be there even when we cannot see it working.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka tells his son Shvetaketu: if someone cuts this great tree at its root, or its middle, or its top, sap flows, but it lives. Full of life, it stands drinking in water. But if life leaves one branch, that branch dries up. The body dies when life leaves it. Life itself does not die.
teachings.link: Uddalaka noticed the same signs we test: the tree drinks, heals and grows, and a dead branch stops doing them. He then asked what life itself is, beyond the signs.

teachings.teaching: Jain teachings name six kinds of living beings: beings of earth, water, fire and air, plants, and beings that move about. All of them can be harmed, so we should harm none of them.
teachings.link: Jain thinkers drew the line of life far wider than science does. It shows that where we draw the line is partly our choice, and the choice changes how we treat the world.

teachings.source: J.C. Bose, Friday Evening Discourse at the Royal Institution, London, 10 May 1901
teachings.teaching: At the end of his talk, Bose said that his records of metals, plants and animals showed him one 'pervading unity' running through all things. He said that thinkers on the banks of the Ganga had taught this about three thousand years before.
teachings.link: Bose was a scientist who measured carefully. His measurements made him wonder whether living and non-living are two worlds, or one.

science.text: Seeds can stay alive for a very long time. A date palm seed about 2,000 years old, found at Masada in Israel, was sprouted in 2005 and grew into a tree.
How non-living chemicals first became living things, about 4,000 million years ago, is still unknown.

other_view.view: Most biologists say alive or not is a question of cells, energy and passing on instructions, not of awareness. Many would say that a seed, a wire or a stone is not aware at all. They say Bose's tired metal only looks like a living response. That is an honest view, and it is not ours.

practice.title: Seven signs, sitting still
practice.say: Let's sit very still together for one minute. Even now, you are doing the signs of life. Put a hand on your tummy and feel the breath going in and out. Now put two fingers on the side of your neck and feel your heartbeat. Listen for three sounds. That is sensing. Somewhere inside you, a hair is growing and a scratch is healing. You are not making any of it happen. It is just happening. Who is doing it?
practice.kid: Sit very still. Feel your breath go in and out. Feel your heartbeat. Listen for three sounds. Your body is doing life all by itself.

how_we_found_out.story: For thousands of years, people believed that some living things start by themselves from non-living things. Maggots seemed to grow out of rotting meat, and mice out of old grain. This idea is called spontaneous generation. In 1668, Francesco Redi, an Italian doctor, put pieces of meat in jars. He left some jars open and covered others with fine cloth. Flies landed on the open meat, and maggots appeared there. The covered meat rotted too, but no maggots grew on it. So the maggots hatched from eggs laid by flies. Still, many people thought tiny living things, too small to see, could start by themselves in soup. Around 1860, Louis Pasteur, in France, boiled soup in flasks with long, curved necks. Air could get in, but dust and tiny living things stuck in the bend. The soup stayed clear for months. When he snapped a neck off, the soup went cloudy within days. Today, life comes only from life.
how_we_found_out.who: Francesco Redi, an Italian doctor, and Louis Pasteur, a French scientist
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That living things such as maggots, mice and germs can start by themselves from meat, grain or soup. This is called spontaneous generation.
